Oral and maxillofacial surgery · published research

Palatal donor-site wound healing

Some randomized studies report faster wound-area reduction, but outcomes differ and PBM is not consistently superior to active comparators.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some randomized studies report faster wound-area reduction, but outcomes differ and PBM is not consistently superior to active comparators.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact palatal-wound category contains ten unique titles: four human randomized reports and six animal studies. One mouse publication also carries an in-vitro tag, so that tag is not a seventh laboratory cohort. Human trials concern donor sites after gingival or connective-tissue graft harvesting, and their comparators and wound outcomes differ. (Bozkurt and Özdemir 2025 da Silva Neves et al. 2016)

Human and clinical evidence

Four randomized trials are indexed. Bozkurt and Özdemir randomized 36 patients to PBM, injectable platelet-rich fibrin, or control after free gingival graft harvesting. The report found smaller wounds in active-treatment groups than controls at selected days, but it did not establish that PBM was superior to platelet fibrin. A 54-patient dose-comparison trial reported faster wound-area reduction with the 60 J/cm² protocol at day seven. The evidence remains small and outcome-specific.

Animal evidence

Six animal publications are indexed (rat and mouse models), examining palatal or mucosal wound responses.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One in-vitro tag overlaps a mouse study. There is no separate in-vitro patient-tissue cohort in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2025 trial used a 980 nm near-infrared laser over five sessions in 14 days, but fluence and exposure time are not stated in the database record. The 2016 trial used 660 nm visible red light and compared 30 with 60 J/cm² across seven sessions over two weeks. These protocols are not interchangeable, and missing settings should not be inferred.

Interpretation

Small randomized studies suggest that PBM may improve selected wound-area or pain outcomes, but active comparators and different follow-up schedules limit a uniform conclusion. Future trials should register dose, standardize wound measurement, report analgesic use and tissue quality, and distinguish PBM effects from platelet products and routine postoperative care.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for palatal wound area and pain Very low for superiority over active comparators

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains ten titles: four human randomized trials and six animal studies, with one in-vitro tag overlapping a mouse study. Clinical outcomes vary by dose and comparator. Further trials should compare PBM with standard care, use blinded wound-area measurement, and report pain and tissue quality.
